content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper tackles music generation and music editing tasks. It uses a novel 2 stages hybrid generation algorithm, using diffusion to generate piano rolls (notes, structure) followed by an autoregressive model performing MIDI event generation (second stage removes artifacts, incorporates performance details, e.g velocity..). Using this two stages allows for easy editing from non experts on the piano rolls that are  more interpretable by humans than MIDI events. The flexibility of the method allows to evaluate the model on various tasks and fine grained music editing.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
__Strong points :__


 - Introduction of a novel two stages generative algorithm on hybrid representations. 
 - Easy editing for non experts on the piano rolls. 
 - The flexible diffusion framework allows for multiple applications using a single set of models. 
 - Clear piano roll visualizations allow for quick understanding of the tasks.

__Weak points__
 - There are too few samples (one sample per task is not enough, different continuations from the same input would be great)
 - The paper lacks comparisons with other methods (e.g. continuations with the same inputs compare to AudioLM https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.03143 for instance). Samples generated from the piano rolls without auto-regressive stage would also be nice. For generation from scratch, comparing the piano roll stage with a simple GAN Based method would be an interesting baseline to compare to. 
 - Would benefit from more ablation to evaluate the impact of two stage generation (for generation from scratch conditional or unconditional). How does generating first the piano roll impacts the MIDI generation? How does it behaves with the MIDI event generator alone ? Some samples to showcase the removal of outliers in the piano roll would help support the claim.  
 - The paper is lacking experiments on other datasets to evaluate the method on more complex music, multi instruments ? 
 - More analysis concerning the piano roll diffusion would be interesting. Computational efficiency ? Schedule choice, number of steps? 

__Additional notes__

 - https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.05944.pdf (unpublished) music inpainting that looks comparable.
 - Not crucial but there are more than two SDEs for score based generative modeling (e.g. sub VP SDE presented by Song et al https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.13456)
 - Might be  clearer for diffusion newcomers to specify that $d\bar w$ is Wiener process for backward time flow. 
 - eq 4 is roughly introduced, would be great to specify that this iteration rule is one discretization of the VP-SDE (derived in song et al) and corresponds to ancestral sampler of ddpm (Ho et al : https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11239).
 - Other than interpretability, why not performing the editing tasks directly on MIDI events ? (There are human friendly ways to display MIDI events.)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clear, the subjective test guidelines are present in the paper. The code is unavailable which makes the experiments not reproducible. The paper includes some novelties but lack experiments and analysis to back up design choices.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper introduced a new ideas that look promising especially regarding easy to use editing for multiple tasks. However it may need more in depth analysis and ablations to evaluate whether the framework is really efficient.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper adapts SDEdit (Meng et al, 2021) to the music domain, demonstrating a diffusion based generative prior plus conditioning signals can support a wide range of music editing interactions, such as stroke-based generation and editing, inpainting, outpainting, etc. To enable this, the paper proposes a two-stage pipeline that combines generative modeling of pianorolls that are intuitive for user editing and an additional decoding module that transforms pianorolls to MIDI-event tokens that have been shown previously to yield compelling results for music generation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 

Adapting methods that work well in other modalities (in this case the visual domain) to music often involves domain-specific challenges and innovations. In particular, how to represent music is still an open problem, with different representations needed for different tasks. This work overcomes this challenge by leveraging a hybrid of representations, based on what is most suitable for users versus generative models. What might be some other differences (from Meng et al, 2022) that could be highlighted?

This work also had to address the challenge of stochastic differential approaches for a discrete domain. More discussion with respect to related efforts in diffusion for music and other discrete domains could yield more insight on the technical novelty and significance of this work.

This paper has the potential to make progress towards the flexible and fine-grained ways of editing for music that were only previously possible in the visual domain. 

Weaknesses:

This paper could benefit from having a contribution section, and discussing how the work is situated and differentiated from prior work in generative assistive editing in other modalities such as visual and text, diffusion approaches for music, scaling up to more complex kinds of music, and generative assistive editing for music specifically. 

The proposed hybrid representation is intuitively well-suited for the proposed tasks. Since it's a two-stage pipeline, would it make sense to include evaluation for each of the stages? Figure 7 shows the output of the first stage, i.e. the diffusion model. Is it expected that the model is not able to "denoise" the extreme high and low notes, and that it's delegated to the second stage to "denoise" those notes? Is the discreteness of the domain making it more challenging? Perhaps this could be discussed or evaluated more.

From the introduction of the paper, the main contribution seems to be in its application to the music domain and how it enables a wide range of music editing interactions. Unfortunately, the demo page (https://SDMuse.github.io/posts/sdmuse/) seems preliminary making it difficult to qualitatively assess the application and domain contributions. For listening to the generated examples, a more guided explanation could be helpful. For example, what might be considered an improvement, if relevant, to listen for? No examples are provided for the "combination" and "style transfer" use cases. For many of the tasks, no prior work examples are given for comparison. Perhaps some examples from the listening test could be included? The outpainting example only shows out painting in the continuation direction, and not yet both directions. 

The stroke-based generation and editing is a very compelling use case, and a nice analogy to the stroke painting and stroke-based editing in prior work SDEdit (Meng et al, 2021). Yet in the music use case, it is less clear what is a user-friendly way to specify music as strokes. The paper does not address this question much. More examples could be given for this task to showcase its creative potential.

Evaluation of generative outputs is difficult, especially in music. The paper focuses the quality evaluation on two metrics, pitch and rhythm distribution distance. Is this sufficient? Perhaps there could be more discussion on this choice with regard to the evaluation metrics proposed in Yang & Lerch, 2018. From the "controllability" axes, this seems to be a natural choice as the conditioning signal relates to these metrics. For Table 3, what are the 95% confidence intervals on the objective PD and DD metrics?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper is clear and well-written. It could be more situated in related work to clarify its contribution and broaden its impact. 

Quality: The paper demonstrates a working generative assistive editing system. More user-centric design could be considered in designing the user interactions. The evaluation is multifaceted, i.e. both objective and subjective. The creative potential of the work could be amplified with more demo examples.

Novelty: The paper presents a novel application of SDEdit (Meng et al, 2021) into the music domain. Some musical tasks such as inpainting and style transfer have been attempted before and it's less clear how the current approach compares, especially qualitatively as examples are not yet provided on the demo page. 

Reproducibility: The music dataset that the paper used is publicly available. The procedures are described in detail. The appendix is informative. Will the code be open sourced?
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper is a novel application of the SDEdit (Meng et al, 2021) to the music domain, with the potential of making progress towards the flexible and fine-grained ways of editing for music that were only previously possible in the visual domain. 

The paper could be strengthened by clarifying its technical contributions, and with more demo examples supporting its empirical novelty and significance.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors propose a two-step method to generate MIDI performances in the style of the ailabs1k7 dataset.
The main idea is to first generate a pianoroll-like intermediate representation called onsetroll (binary matrix with ones where there is a note onset) that will then be "upscaled" to an event-based MIDI-like representation.
The first step is done using a diffusion model which can be conditioned on additional information such as note density or chord progression.
The second one is a done with a Transformer decoder conditioned on the generated onsetroll.
The objective of this approach is to leverage the generation capabilities of diffusion models like the one showcased in the SDEedit paper.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- Strength: the idea to use an intermediate representation amenable to be generated with a diffusion model is interesting, as this allows to directly transpose SDEedit techniques from image to onsetrolls. This provides a way to perform stroke-based editing and generation for instance. The audio examples in the accompanying website sound nicely, but are hard to understand.

- Weakness: Diffusion model on binary data is not straightforward, and the relevant literature is not discussed at all.
More generally, the discussion about the related works in music generation omits too many relevant works. These omissions make it difficult to understand the novelties of this approach for a reader external to the field.
For instance: - Mittal et al. 2021 use a diffusion model to generate symbolic music, it would be valuable to discuss how this differs from the proposed approach
- symbolic music inpainting was already considered in many works, how are these different from the proposed approach, and why these approaches are not cited?
- Musenet, which can be considered as state-of-the-art for unconditional generation is not cited as well.
Properly discussing these approaches would make the motivation behind this work clearer.
Also, this makes some claims such as "So far, no one has explored editing musical pieces at fine granularity in the same flexible way as image editing, such as inpainting (Pathak et al., 2016) and outpainting (Wang et al., 2014)." wrong and misleading. 

Limitations not properly addressed and the subjective evaluation does not seem significant. The outputs of the diffusion model seem to contain lots of wrong notes (see Fig. 7). On the one hand, it is interesting to see that the Transformer decoder is able to remove these wrong notes, on the other hand, it clearly shows the limitations of the diffusion-based approach on such data. Were the onsetroll outputs of the diffusion model plausible, it would only suffice to consider a Transformer decoder to predict offset deviation, duration and velocity for each note. Many works on this topic already exist in the literature and have not been cited (expressive score rendering). Also, it is quite surprising that the Transformer decoder has this behavior since it was trained on clean onsetrolls with no outliers. It also means that it is impossible for a user to only use the second stage to transform onset rolls to expressive MIDI performances as some notes could be replaced, or erased.
It should also be stated that despite the numerous generation capabilities offered by this model, some musical edits are not available due to the two-stage nature of the framework (like conditioning on velocities or generating based on user-defined velocity curves).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This article requires prior knowledge in the related works as some details may not be clear and the article is not self-contained.
Many terms should also be defined or exemplified before their use like fine-grained music  editing, stroke-based editing (cite Fig. 2b for instance), pianoroll (many pianoroll representations exists + the authors only consider so-called onsetrolls).

Part 2.3 is not self-contained for readers who do not know score-based models (what is the training loss for instance).


Fig1 is unclear: the exact same sequence could be used for all three representations, a simpler score could be used,  representation in (c) does not look like the representation in Fig. 2 (a).
Caption in Fig. 2 
Fig. 3 we cannot draw any conclusion from Fig. 3
Fig. 7: there are some held notes in Fig. 7 (a) while it is supposed to be an onsetroll.
Fig. 8 is unclear: seems to be drawn only for one example and examples are stochastic as seen in Alg. 1. It seems impossible to see the difference between the different embedding methods.

Some terms could be more detailed to better guide the reader
Music -> symbolic music / MIDI data
Refinement -> Regeneration
Difference between pianoroll and MIDI-event representations ->  without velocity + on grid 
"indiscriminate treatment of note onsets and other positions" -> 
Notations:
c_n becomes s_n  in Fig. 2
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper proposes an interesting approach, but the technical contribution is quite incremental. The significance of the proposed method is weakened by the absence of a proper discussion with the related works.
It seems like a novel iteration of the methods shown in Tab. 3.
The related work seems quite biased towards specific authors. This prevents a fair comparison with other works to take place and finally does not help understanding how this paper differs from other approaches.

content.title: SDMuse: Stochastic Differential Music Editing and Generation via Hybrid Representation
content.abstract:
While deep generative models have empowered music generation, it remains a challenging and under-explored problem to edit an existing musical piece at fine granularity.
In this paper, we propose SDMuse, a unified stochastic differential music editing and generation framework, which can not only compose a whole musical piece from scratch, but also modify existing musical pieces in many ways, such as combination, continuation, inpainting, and style transferring.
The proposed SDMuse follows a two-stage pipeline to achieve music generation and editing on top of a hybrid representation including pianoroll and MIDI-event.
In particular, SDMuse first generates/edits pianoroll by iteratively denoising through a stochastic differential equation (SDE) based on a diffusion model generative prior, and then refines the generated pianoroll and predicts MIDI-event tokens auto-regressively.
We evaluate the generated music of our method on ailabs1k7 pop music dataset in terms of quality and controllability on various music editing and generation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed stochastic differential music editing and generation process, as well as the hybrid representations.
